blocks.text: Saint George is the patron saint of England, and of many other countries, and Christians still honor him today. The Golden Legend, a book of saints' lives put together by the Italian bishop Jacobus de Voragine, tells his story. This is its part about the dragon; afterwards the book tells how George died for his faith, which is left out here.
Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend: Saint George

George, a tribune, an officer of the Roman army, who came from a family of Cappadocia, once came into the province of Libya, to a city called Silena. Near this city was a lake as big as a sea, and in it lurked a deadly dragon. It had often driven back the people when they armed themselves against it, and when it came up to the walls of the city, it poisoned everyone with its breath. So the citizens were forced to give it two sheep every day to calm its fury; otherwise it would come up to the walls of the city and poison the air, so that very many people died.

When the sheep were nearly all gone, because they could not find enough of them, the people took counsel and gave the dragon a sheep and a person with it. So the sons and daughters of the people were chosen by lot, and the lot spared no one. When nearly all the sons and daughters had been eaten, one day the lot fell on the king's only daughter, and she was given to the dragon. Then the king, full of sorrow, said: "Take gold and silver and half my kingdom, and let my daughter go, so that she does not die like this." The people answered him in fury: "You, O king, made this law, and now all our children are dead, and you want to save your own daughter! Unless you do to your daughter what you ordered for the others, we will burn you and your house."

When the king saw this, he began to weep for his daughter, saying: "Alas, my sweetest daughter, what shall I do with you? What shall I say? When shall I ever see your wedding?" And turning to the people, he said: "I beg you, give me eight days to mourn my daughter." The people allowed it, but at the end of the eight days they came back in fury, saying: "Why are you destroying your people for the sake of your daughter? See, we are all dying from the dragon's breath."

Then the king, seeing that he could not save his daughter, dressed her in royal clothes, and embraced her with tears, and said: "Alas, my sweetest daughter, I thought I would rock your children in my royal lap, and now you are going to be eaten by the dragon. Alas, my sweetest daughter, I hoped to invite princes to your wedding, to adorn the palace with pearls, to hear drums and organs; and now you are going to be eaten by the dragon." And he kissed her and let her go, saying: "Oh, my daughter, if only I had died before you, rather than lose you like this!" Then she fell at her father's feet and asked for his blessing, and when her father had blessed her with tears, she went out to the lake.

Blessed George happened to be passing that way, and when he saw her weeping, he asked her what was wrong. She said: "Good young man, get on your horse quickly and flee, so that you do not die with me." George said to her: "Do not be afraid, my daughter, but tell me what you are waiting for here, with all the people watching." She said: "I can see, good young man, that you have a great heart. But do you want to die with me? Flee, quickly!" George said: "I will not leave this place until you tell me what is wrong." So she told him everything, and George said: "My daughter, do not be afraid, for in the name of Christ I will help you." And she said: "Good knight, hurry and save yourself; do not perish with me. It is enough if I die alone. You could not save me, and you would die with me."

While they were speaking, look! the dragon came and lifted its head out of the lake. The girl, trembling, said: "Flee, good lord, flee quickly!" Then George mounted his horse, and making the sign of the cross to protect himself, he boldly charged at the dragon as it came at him. He swung his lance with all his strength and, commending himself to God, he wounded it badly and threw it to the ground. And he said to the girl: "Throw your belt around the dragon's neck, my daughter, and do not be afraid."

When she had done this, the dragon followed her like the gentlest of dogs. So she led it into the city; and when the people saw it, they began to flee over the mountains and hills, crying: "Woe to us, for now we shall all die!" Then blessed George waved to them, saying: "Do not be afraid, for the Lord has sent me to you to free you from the torment of the dragon. Only believe in Christ, and let each of you be baptized, and I will kill this dragon." Then the king and all the people were baptized, and blessed George drew his sword and killed the dragon, and ordered it to be carried out of the city. Four pairs of oxen dragged it out into a great field. That day twenty thousand were baptized, not counting the little children and the women.

The king built a church of wonderful size in honor of blessed Mary and blessed George, and from its altar a living spring flows, whose water heals all who are sick. The king offered blessed George a great fortune, but he would not take it, and ordered it to be given to the poor. Then George taught the king four things in a few words: to take care of God's churches, to honor the priests, to listen faithfully to the services, and always to remember the poor. And so he kissed the king and went away. But in some books it is written that as the dragon was coming to eat the girl, George made the sign of the cross, attacked the dragon and killed it.

Translated by Claude (Anthropic), 2026, from the Latin of Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend (Legenda Aurea, about 1260), as published by The Latin Library and collected in the Classical Language Toolkit's Latin corpus.
